Accelerating Growth

Analysing the UK’s leading startup accelerator programme

A variety of ways to grow
We use eight criteria to identify high-growth and 
ambitious companies. Each of these is a sign of external 
validation that a business is either actively growing or 
creating ambitious growth plans. 
Attending an accelerator is just one method of growth. 
Companies can attain any number or combination of 
these growth methods. 
Every company included in this report has attended an 
accelerator programme, and may or may not have hit 
additional tracking triggers.

What is an accelerator?
Simply put, an accelerator oﬀers programmes to help 
startups grow. 
The number of these programmes has grown dramatically in 
the last few years, with accelerators specialising in niche 
verticals and specific stages of company growth. 
We believe (and our data shows) attending an accelerator is 
a good indicator of a company’s potential to grow.
But with such a wide variety of accelerators and related 
programmes like incubators, startup studios and co-working 
spaces, it can be diﬀicult to tell which of these programmes 
are true indicators of future success. 
As such, we have a selection of strict criteria that each 
programme must meet in order to be included in our data →  
The duration is a set period of time
The programme has a clear structure
The application process is competitive
There are no (or minimal) joining fees
To be included in our analysis, accelerators 
must meet the following criteria:

Building partnerships
We’ve found that an increasing number of businesses are 
wanting to track and approach accelerator programmes and 
their alumni. 
Building relationships with their cohort from an early stage 
can lead to long lasting business relationships, that become 
increasing lucrative as the young companies continue to 
grow and fulfil their potential. 
Some providers to high-growth companies also like to build 
partnerships with the accelerators themselves, 
strengthening their reputation and consolidating their 
relationship with each new year of applicants.

There are a range of diﬀerent accelerators across the UK 
with diﬀerent specialisations and areas of expertise. But the 
vast majority of programmes are focused on nurturing 
young, seed stage startups. 
82% of companies are in the seed stage when they join a 
programme. 
Just 4% are in the growth stage of evolution, but there are 
some big players operating in this part of the market. 
For example, ELITE oﬀers a programme of structured 
engagement to growing UK companies, supporting them to 
develop for the next stages of growth and investment. The 
majority of companies that the programme has supported 
were in the growth (35%) or established (18%) stages of 
evolution when they joined.
Stages of evolution
Stages of evolution of companies at start date

Acceleration programmes are all about getting a company 
oﬀ the ground and giving them the tools they need to 
realise their full potential. These are usually high intensity 
courses, with 27% lasting just three months. This is the 
conventional duration, and the one used by high-profile 
names like Y-Combinator and Techstars. 
The second most common programme period is six months, 
followed by a year. 
Of all the 158 accelerators we track, just five are scheduled 
for longer than a year. The accelerator with the longest 
duration is the Future Fifty programme, which supports 
businesses for up to two years. 
Programme length
Most common lengths of UK accelerator programmes

Each accelerator is unique, operating in diﬀerent markets 
and providing an assortment of perks and benefits. 
By far the most common of these is mentoring, where 
founders receive one-to-one support, advice and training. Of 
all active accelerators, 84% provide this perk.
As the old adage goes, it’s not what you know, but who you 
know that counts. Accelerators are master introducers, with 
access to business networks, industry experts, and investor 
networks the next three most popular benefits. 
Perks and benefits
Most common benefits oﬀered by UK accelerators

We’ve always had excellent feedback from our peer to peer networking sessions… 
it’s not often you have the opportunity to speak to such a range of C suite execs who 
have faced similar challenges themselves and therefore learn from their mistakes 
and successes. More broadly, we’ve heard that the Future Fifty accolade in itself has 
massively helped our attendees with recruitment and investment. 
Parveen Dhanda, Tech Nation,  UK Unicorns: Britain’s $1b Businesses

On their own, accelerators help few companies to the next 
stage of evolution. Of all the companies that attended an 
accelerator in 2015 and have not used any other methods of 
growth, just 2% have progressed to a later stage of growth, 
and only 1% have exited the market. The majority have 
stagnated, showing little growth since graduating. A massive 
44% have not survived the last five years. 
As a point of comparison, companies that received equity 
backing in 2015 and have not used any other methods of 
growth are five times as likely to have progressed and six 
times as likely to have exited. But stagnation and death 
rates still remain relatively high. 
Companies that have accessed accelerators in 2015 and 
secured other forms of support or achieved further external 
validation have seen the most improvement in this cohort. 
Success rates
Success rates of companies that accessed support in 2015

Around a third of accelerator programmes have the backing 
of a corporation, such as Barclays Accelerator, managed by 
Techstars, and Geovation’s PropTech Programme, 
sponsored by Ordnance Survey and HM Land Registry.
Backing from an organisation enhances the reputation of 
the accelerator, whilst also providing attendees with a 
valuable opportunity to meet contacts from the business.
Accelerators that have the backing of a corporation have far 
higher success rates than those that don’t. 
Of the companies that attended a corporate-sponsored 
accelerator in 2015, a third have gone on to further stages 
of growth, and 9% have exited the market, either through an 
IPO or an acquisition. 
Corporate sponsors
Success rates of companies that attended an accelerator 
programme in 2015 by sponsorship status

“Among the many benefits of our programmes is the corporate validation that they 
can provide for young companies developing new and innovative technologies. 
Validation from an industry leader can make all the diﬀerence when it comes to 
winning future investment.”
“We ran our first programme, JLAB, with John Lewis in 2014. A few corporates 
sponsored accelerators at that time, but none truly collaborated with startups. We 
saw a gap in the market for programmes where startups can work closely with 
corporates to develop and trial products. The corporate is fully engaged and 
experiences technologies which have the potential to transform their business.”
L Marks, Accelerating the UK

Geography
Unsurprisingly, London has the highest number of 
accelerators in the UK — 59% reside in the Capital. But 
companies travel from far and wide to access the right 
accelerator programme. 
Accelerators are a particularly popular method of growth for 
companies in Northern Ireland, where 41% of all 
high-growth companies have attended an accelerator, and 
Scotland, where that figure stands at 43%.
An impressive 14% of accelerated companies are registered 
in Scotland, which is mostly due to the Royal Bank of 
Scotland’s Entrepreneur Accelerator network. This ran for 
three years in partnership with Entrepreneurial Spark. At the 
beginning of 2018, the bank brought the fully-funded 
programme in-house.

The most common buzzwords associated with accelerator 
programmes are artificial intelligence and fintech. 
Companies operating within these spaces get a lot of 
attention from investors and, consequently, the media. 
There are now a number of programmes in place specifically 
catered to these verticals. 
For example, AI for Good is a four-month programme for 
businesses, charities and NGOs developing AI in the areas of 
earth, accessibility, cultural heritage or humanitarian action. 
Run by Social Tech Trust and sponsored by Microsoft, it’s 
supported 19 companies over the past two years. 
Fintech Innovation Lab London oﬀers mentoring, workshops 
and networking opportunities to fintech startups, and is 
backed by multinational consultancy firm Accenture. 
Buzzwords
Top tech sectors by number of accelerator attendees

“Nimble accelerators should continuously evolve to stay relevant — from 
specialising in a particular stage of growth of the startup process to entering 
emerging markets, and focusing on partnerships with corporations.”
Startupbootcamp, Accelerating the UK

Over half of all high-growth businesses founded by 
all-female teams have grown using the support of an 
accelerator. This is the most popular method of growth for 
female-led businesses. So, why might this be?
We all know that female founders are less likely to raise 
finance than male founders, so it makes sense that they’re 
accessing alternative modes of support. 
Female founders may be drawn to the extra value and 
transparency that comes with a structured accelerator 
programme, rather than transactional methods of growth. 
There are also a selection of programmes built for female 
founders, to support them through the specific challenges 
they face, such as Hatch’s Female Founders programme. 
Female founders
Proportion of high-growth companies that have attended 
an accelerator programme by gender of founding team

“We've seen female founders opening up about their struggles and challenges to 
each other, especially as many have to survive and thrive in male-dominated 
environments. For example, it can be frustrating if you've got a female-specific 
product or service but you're only ever pitching to men. 
Having a supportive group of fellow female founders around you can really help with 
relevant advice, sharing insights and best practices, as well as relevant contacts.”
Dirk Bischof, Hatch Enterprises, Female Entrepreneurs

Top 5 Accelerators in the UK
By number of total attendances

As the successor to the Entrepreneurial Spark 
programme, Entrepreneur Accelerator is a six-month 
programme run by NatWest, operating under the RBS 
brand in Scotland and Ulster Bank in Northern Ireland.
Through 12 programme hubs across the UK, attendees 
receive free oﬀice space, 1:1 coaching, bespoke events, as 
well as access to mentors, legal advice, its business 
networks and supply chains. Whilst the programme is 
fully-funded, Entrepreneur Accelerator does not take any 
equity.
Businesses can attend the accelerator up to three times, 
lasting a possible 18 months in total. Entrepreneur 
Accelerator has had 2300 attendances to date, with seven 
successful exits including Hyre, Bold and Pouch.

This free, three-month programme supports 
London-based SMEs through mentoring schemes, 
workshops, and tailored growth plans, alongside 
opportunities to collaborate with large corporates. 
Following graduation from the programme, businesses 
have access to exclusive events.
In order to apply to the programme, companies must 
first be registered in the UK, have between three and 250 
employees, be based in — and looking to grow across — 
London, and have a turnover of less than £40m. 
The programme has had 511 attendees, with three exits 
from Dovetail Lab, Synergy, and The Booking Factory.
2    Business Growth Programme

UENI

PwC Scale Programmes currently runs seven 
programmes: LawTech, Retail, Cyber, FinTech, 
PropTech, and Aerospace, Defence & Security, plus a 
programme focused on business in the South East.
Each lasts ten weeks and consists of three core 
elements: curated events (like group masterclasses), 
individual coaching, and bespoke business support.
PwC Scale Programmes charge a fixed fee for 
attendance, the cost of which varies between its 
programmes. 
To date, the accelerator has had 193 attendances and 
nine successful exits. 
3    PwC Scale Programmes
Manager  PwC Scale Programmes
Location  London
Total attendees  193
Notable attendees

Entrepreneur First matches ambitious individuals with 
potential co-founders.
Alongside team building and idea generation, attendees 
receive funding from day one, the opportunity to pitch 
to the investment committee, and expert training.
To date, the London-based accelerator has supported 
187 attendees, 121 of which have gone on to secure 
investment, with an average amount of £67k.
There have been ten successful exits by attendee 
companies, including Magic Pony Technology, bought 
out by Twitter for $150m in 2016, 18 months after its 
founders met on the programme.

Future Fifty provides late-stage growth programmes, 
specifically aimed at the UK’s leading tech businesses. 
Managed by Tech Nation, the two-year programme 
provides peer-to-peer learning networks, masterclass 
workshops led by global experts, as well as sessions with 
government oﬀicials and ministerial roundtables. 
To apply, businesses must have at least £5m in revenues 
or have raised a minimum of Series B in funding and can 
prove 50% year-on-year growth.
The Future Fifty accelerator has had 169 attendees to 
date, with 37 successful exits worth a combined £5.25b.

Entrepreneur First matches ambitious individuals with
potential co-founders.
Alongside team building and idea generation, attendees
receive funding from day one, the opportunity to pitch
to the investment committee, and expert training.
To date, the London-based accelerator has supported
187 attendees, 121 of which have gone on to secure
investment, with an average amount of £67k.
There have been ten successful exits by attendee
companies, including Magic Pony Technology, bought
out by Twitter for $150m in 2016, 18 months after its
founders met on the programme.

Future Fifty provides late-stage growth programmes,
specifically aimed at the UK’s leading tech businesses.
Managed by Tech Nation, the two-year programme
provides peer-to-peer learning networks, masterclass
workshops led by global experts, as well as sessions with
government officials and ministerial roundtables.
To apply, businesses must have at least £5m in revenues
or have raised a minimum of Series B in funding and can
prove 50% year-on-year growth.
The Future Fifty accelerator has had 169 attendees to
date, with 37 successful exits worth a combined £5.25b.
